summary: This best current practice documents the syntax used in YANG module tree diagrams, the compact text pictures of a module's structure. It gathers the definition in one place so authors and readers can interpret the diagrams consistently. The syntax may be updated over time as YANG evolves.

plainLanguage.summary: YANG tree diagrams show the structure of a network data model using short text lines and symbols. RFC 8340 defines how to read those symbols so documents can use one shared notation.

subtitle: A shared guide to the symbols and layout used in YANG tree diagrams.

tldr.problem: Documents that include YANG tree diagrams often repeat the explanation of their symbols. Repeated explanations can differ and make diagrams harder to interpret consistently.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8340 defines a shared text notation for module trees, node names, status, flags, options, types, features and mounted schemas.
tldr.outcome: Authors can refer to one definition, which the RFC expects may change as YANG evolves. RFC 8340 is a Best Current Practice updated by RFC 8791.

today: RFC 8340 is a Best Current Practice and is updated by RFC 8791. The RFC says the notation may change as the YANG language evolves.

sections.title: Why the Notation Has One Definition
sections.content:
A YANG tree diagram gives a simplified view of a data model. Tools such as pyang can generate the diagrams.

RFC 8340 gathers the notation in one place instead of having every document define it again. The RFC expects this definition may be updated or replaced as YANG changes.
sections.plainLanguage: A tree diagram is a compact text view of a YANG data model. This RFC gives documents one shared definition of its symbols.

sections.title: The Shape of a Tree Diagram
sections.content:
A full module tree starts with module: and the module name. Sections then appear in a defined order: top-level data nodes, augmentations, RPCs, notifications, groupings and yang-data structures.

Each node begins with +--. A child sits three spaces to the right of its parent. Vertical bars connect siblings when other lines appear between them. A submodule uses the same layout but starts with submodule:.
sections.plainLanguage: The diagram starts with the module name and lists its kinds of content in a set order. Indentation shows parent and child nodes.

sections.title: Status, Flags and Node Details
sections.content:
A node line follows this pattern: <status>--<flags> <name><options> <type> <if-features>. The status is + for current, x for deprecated or o for obsolete.

Flags describe the node, such as rw for configuration data, ro for read-only data, -x for an RPC or action, and -n for a notification. Options include ? for an optional node, ! for a presence container and an asterisk after a name for a list or leaf-list. The remaining fields show its name, type and any feature dependencies.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line tells you whether a node is current, what kind of node it is, and whether it can be changed. It can also show the node's type and feature requirements.

sections.title: Keeping Diagrams Readable in Documents
sections.content:
RFCs and Internet-Drafts limit lines to 72 characters. Authors should break a long node line between its options and type, or between its type and feature list, and indent the continued line beneath the name.

Long diagrams can be divided into smaller trees, such as separate diagrams for data nodes and notifications. A diagram longer than a page should generally be avoided, and authors can place a long diagram in an appendix.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep each line within the document's width. If the whole tree is too long, split it into smaller diagrams.

sections.title: Showing Mounted Schemas
sections.content:
A schema mount lets a server provide YANG modules at a mount point in a parent schema. A container or list can be a mount point, and the diagram marks it with the mp flag.

The server determines which modules appear under the mount point. In the diagram, mounted modules are shown much like content from a grouping. A slash marks a mounted module's top-level node; an at sign marks a top-level node reached through a parent reference. The schema-mount module's config value determines whether mounted nodes are shown as configurable or read-only.
sections.plainLanguage: A mount point marks where a server can provide another schema. The diagram uses extra symbols to show mounted nodes and whether they are configurable.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 8340 says the tree diagrams have no security impact. The document also makes no requests for IANA action.

The diagrams describe data-model structure; they do not define a network protocol or a security mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: This document defines a way to draw YANG models. It reports no security impact and requests no IANA action.

data.title: Interface nodes
data.code:
+--rw interfaces
   +--rw interface* [name]
      +--rw name                        string
      +--rw description?                string
      +--rw type                        identityref
      +--rw enabled?                    boolean
      +--rw link-up-down-trap-enable?   enumeration {if-mib}?
